To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
C2 cleavage occurs when C2 binds to C4b on a target surface and that C4b2a is a stable, active C3 convertase.
the C2 cleavage is a limiting step in complement activation, and that the C3 convertase activity is regulated by the C3b-binding site on C2a.

we have purified C2 from human serum, that the purified C2 is active as a C3 convertase, that C1s is able to cleave C2 in the fluid phase, and that the cleavage of C2 by C1s is a limiting step in complement activation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the isolation of the complement components, the characterization of their interactions, and the elucidation of the mechanism of activation of the classical pathway.
the study of the structure of the C2 protein, the mechanism of C2 activation by C1s, C1r2-CIs2, and C1s2, and the role of C2 in the activation of C3 and C4.
the study of the molecular basis of complement activation and the role of complement in the inflammatory response.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
C2 is a glycoprotein of Mr 105,000, composed of two polypeptide chains (A and 8) linked by disulphide bonds.
the classical pathway of the complement system can be divided into three phases.

the classical pathway of the complement system is a complex cascade system that is initiated by a complex of three proteins, the first component of complement (C1), which is activated by a complex of two proteins, Clq and Clr2, and the fourth component of complement (Clr2).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the C2 molecule is a dimer of 2 nonidentical subunits, each with a molecular weight of approximately 110,000, linked by disulfide bonds.
C2 can be purified to homogeneity from human serum in a single step using affinity chromatography.

the C2 preparation is free from C4, C5 and C6 and has an activity in the fluid phase cleavage of C2 by C1s, C1rs-C1s2 and 1s of about 1000 times the activity of C2 in the C3 convertase complex with C4b.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the complement cascade is an evolutionarily ancient system that predates vertebrates and is likely to have been involved in multicellular life from its inception.
the complement system plays a critical role in the immune system, but it is also a key player in the development and progression of autoimmune diseases.
C2 is an extremely stable molecule.
